diseases.name: Newcastle Disease
diseases.first_aid: Immediately isolate all sick birds. No curative treatment exists. Cull severely affected birds humanely. Disinfect the entire poultry house. Do NOT move birds in or out of the farm.
diseases.treatment: No antiviral treatment. Supportive care only: clean water with electrolytes and vitamins. Antibiotics only to prevent secondary bacterial infections, under veterinary guidance.
biosecurity_actions: Isolate affected birds immediately
Restrict farm access to essential personnel only
Disinfect footwear and equipment at entry points
Do not share equipment with neighbouring farms
Dispose of dead birds by deep burial or incineration
Do not sell birds or eggs from affected flock
diseases.prevention: Vaccinate with La Sota (eye drop or drinking water) at day 1 and day 14. Booster every 3 months. Quarantine new birds for 2 weeks before introduction.
diseases.vaccination_notes: La Sota live vaccine at day 1 and day 14 via eye drop. Inactivated oil-emulsion booster at 6-8 weeks for layers. Repeat every 3 months. Cold chain must be maintained.
diseases.when_to_call_vet: Immediately. Newcastle is a notifiable disease in Nigeria. Any suspected outbreak must be reported to the nearest veterinary office.

diseases.name: Gumboro Disease
diseases.first_aid: Isolate affected birds. Provide clean water immediately with oral rehydration salts. Reduce stress by lowering light intensity. Remove wet litter immediately.
diseases.treatment: No antiviral treatment. Supportive: electrolytes, vitamins A D E K in water. Broad-spectrum antibiotics only to control secondary infections.
biosecurity_actions: Isolate affected pen immediately
The IBD virus survives in the environment for months — full disinfection required
Remove and replace all litter
Fumigate with formaldehyde or approved disinfectant before restocking
Do not allow visitors to affected pen
diseases.prevention: Vaccinate at day 14-18 using IBD live vaccine in drinking water. Booster at day 28. Ensure biosecurity as virus survives months in environment.
diseases.vaccination_notes: IBD intermediate live vaccine at day 14-18 via drinking water. Withhold water 1-2 hours before vaccination. Booster at day 28. Maternal antibodies may interfere — timing critical.
diseases.when_to_call_vet: If mortality exceeds 5% within 48 hours or if secondary infections are suspected.

diseases.name: Coccidiosis
diseases.first_aid: Start anticoccidial treatment immediately. Amprolium is the first-line drug. Remove and replace wet litter. Ensure drinkers and feeders are clean and dry.
diseases.treatment: Amprolium 20%: 30ml per 10 litres of water for 5-7 days. Alternative: Toltrazuril (Baycox) 1ml per litre for 2 consecutive days. Follow with vitamins K and B-complex.
biosecurity_actions: Keep litter dry at all times
Repair leaking drinkers immediately
Reduce stocking density
Clean and disinfect housing between flocks
Rotate anticoccidials to prevent resistance
diseases.prevention: Keep litter dry. Use coccidiostats in starter feed. Avoid overcrowding. Clean between flocks.
diseases.vaccination_notes: Coccivac (live oocyst vaccine) available for broilers. Not widely used in Nigeria. Anticoccidials in feed remain standard prevention.
diseases.when_to_call_vet: If mortality continues after 48 hours of treatment or if cecal coccidiosis (Eimeria tenella) is suspected.
diseases.mortality_rate: Variable by Eimeria species. Eimeria tenella (cecal form) highest mortality.

diseases.name: Fowl Typhoid
diseases.first_aid: Isolate sick birds. Collect dead birds for post-mortem. Do not use eggs from affected flocks. Notify a veterinarian.
diseases.treatment: Enrofloxacin 10mg/kg body weight in water for 5 days. Alternative: Trimethoprim-Sulphonamide for 5-7 days. Treatment reduces mortality but does not eliminate carrier state.
biosecurity_actions: Remove and isolate affected birds immediately
Strict rodent control — rodents are major vectors
Disinfect drinkers and feeders daily
Do not hatch eggs from affected breeding flocks
Test breeding flocks regularly for Salmonella
diseases.prevention: Source birds from Salmonella-free hatcheries. Vaccinate breeding stock with 9R live vaccine where available. Strict rodent control.
diseases.vaccination_notes: 9R live attenuated vaccine for breeding flocks. Not routinely used in commercial broiler production. Biosecurity and sourcing remain primary prevention.
diseases.when_to_call_vet: Immediately. Fowl Typhoid is a notifiable disease. Zoonotic risk exists for humans handling infected birds.
diseases.mortality_rate: 10-50% acute form; chronic form causes persistent losses
diseases.zoonotic_note: Salmonella Gallinarum can infect immunocompromised humans. Handle dead birds with gloves and wash hands thoroughly.

diseases.name: Marek's Disease
symptoms: one leg forward one leg back
distinguishing_symptoms: one leg forward one leg back
diseases.first_aid: No treatment. Separate paralysed birds to prevent trampling. Provide food and water within reach. Cull birds that cannot eat or drink independently.
diseases.treatment: No curative treatment. Supportive care only. Culling affected birds reduces virus shedding.
biosecurity_actions: Vaccinate ALL chicks within 24 hours of hatch — this is the only effective prevention
Marek's virus spreads via feather dust — maintain strict ventilation controls
Clean and disinfect thoroughly between flocks
Do not mix vaccinated and unvaccinated birds
diseases.prevention: Vaccinate ALL chicks at hatchery within 24 hours of hatch with HVT or bivalent Rispens + HVT vaccine. Vaccine prevents disease but not infection.
diseases.vaccination_notes: HVT (Herpesvirus of Turkeys) vaccine at day 1 subcutaneous injection. Bivalent Rispens + HVT preferred for high-pressure environments. Must be given before any exposure — does not treat existing infection.
diseases.when_to_call_vet: When progressive paralysis appears in multiple birds. Necropsy required to confirm diagnosis.
diseases.mortality_rate: Up to 100% in unvaccinated susceptible flocks
references: NVRI Nigeria Marek's Disease Technical Note

diseases.name: Fowl Cholera
diseases.first_aid: Start antibiotic treatment immediately. Isolate affected birds. Provide clean water. Remove dead birds immediately and dispose safely.
diseases.treatment: Penicillin or Tetracycline in water for 5-7 days. Sulphonamides also effective. Continue treatment for 2-3 days after apparent recovery to prevent relapse.
biosecurity_actions: Remove and dispose of dead birds immediately by burial or incineration
Strict rodent and wild bird control — major reservoir hosts
Disinfect all equipment and water sources
Restrict farm access
Do not allow wet conditions — Pasteurella thrives in wet environments
diseases.prevention: Bacterin vaccines available but provide limited cross-protection. Biosecurity and rodent control are primary prevention. Avoid stress, overcrowding and wet litter.
diseases.vaccination_notes: Pasteurella multocida bacterin available. Efficacy varies by serotype. Consult veterinarian for appropriate strain. Biosecurity remains most effective prevention.
diseases.when_to_call_vet: Immediately on suspicion. Mortality can be very rapid in peracute form.
diseases.mortality_rate: Up to 100% in peracute form; 20-50% in acute form

diseases.name: Infectious Bronchitis
distinguishing_symptoms: drop in egg production with respiratory signs
diseases.first_aid: No specific treatment. Provide warmth. Reduce stocking density. Add vitamins and electrolytes to water. Antibiotics for secondary bacterial infection only.
diseases.treatment: Supportive: vitamins, electrolytes. Broad-spectrum antibiotics (Tylosin, Doxycycline) to prevent secondary E. coli or Mycoplasma infection. Keep birds warm.
biosecurity_actions: Improve ventilation without creating draughts
Reduce stocking density
Disinfect drinking water
Separate young chicks from older birds
diseases.prevention: Vaccinate with live IB vaccine (Massachusetts and 4/91 strains) at day 1 and day 14 via spray or drinking water. Booster at 6 weeks.
diseases.vaccination_notes: Live H120 (Massachusetts strain) at day 1 and day 14. 4/91 strain booster at 4-6 weeks for layers. Multiple strains circulate — local strain matching important. Annual review of vaccination programme recommended.
diseases.when_to_call_vet: If egg production does not recover within 3 weeks or if nephropathogenic strain is suspected (increased mortality, wet droppings).
diseases.mortality_rate: Low in adults; up to 25% in young unprotected chicks

diseases.name: Avian Influenza
diseases.first_aid: DO NOT HANDLE DEAD BIRDS WITHOUT PROTECTIVE EQUIPMENT. Immediately report to the nearest veterinary authority. Do not move any birds. Restrict all farm access.
diseases.treatment: No treatment. HPAI requires immediate government response and controlled culling. This is a notifiable disease.
biosecurity_actions: IMMEDIATE REPORTABLE DISEASE — notify veterinary authority now
Do not move birds, eggs, litter or equipment off the farm
Wear gloves and face covering when handling dead birds
Restrict all access to farm — human and vehicle
Do not sell birds or products from affected farm
diseases.prevention: Strict biosecurity. Prevent contact with wild birds. Vaccination available in some countries but not standard in Nigeria. Biosecurity is the primary prevention.
diseases.vaccination_notes: AI vaccination programmes exist (H5N1, H5N2 inactivated vaccines) but are government-controlled in Nigeria. Contact Federal Department of Livestock Services.
diseases.when_to_call_vet: IMMEDIATELY. Avian Influenza is a Class A notifiable disease. Delay in reporting is a legal offence in Nigeria.
diseases.mortality_rate: Up to 100% in HPAI-affected flocks within 48 hours
diseases.zoonotic_note: H5N1 and H5N8 strains can infect humans. Do not handle dead birds without PPE. Seek medical attention if fever develops after exposure.
references: Federal Ministry of Agriculture Nigeria AI Contingency Plan

diseases.name: Infectious Coryza
diseases.first_aid: Treat with antibiotics immediately. Sulphonamides or Erythromycin are first-line. Separate affected birds. Improve ventilation.
diseases.treatment: Sulphadimethoxine in water for 5-7 days. Alternatively Erythromycin or Doxycycline. Treat entire flock as subclinical carriers may exist.
biosecurity_actions: Isolate affected birds immediately
Improve ventilation — Avibacterium spreads via respiratory droplets
Disinfect drinkers and feeders
Do not mix birds of different ages
Birds that recover remain carriers — do not introduce recovered birds to clean flocks
diseases.prevention: All-in all-out management. Do not introduce birds from unknown sources. Bacterin vaccines available in some markets. Reduce stress and ammonia levels.
diseases.vaccination_notes: Inactivated bacterin vaccines available in some markets. Protect only against homologous serotypes (A, B, C). Consult veterinarian for local serotype.
diseases.when_to_call_vet: If swelling spreads to involve the neck or if antibiotic treatment shows no response within 48 hours.
diseases.mortality_rate: Low mortality but severe production losses. Morbidity can reach 100%.

diseases.name: Chronic Respiratory Disease
diseases.first_aid: Begin antibiotic treatment. Tylosin or Doxycycline are first-line for Mycoplasma. Reduce stocking density and improve ventilation.
diseases.treatment: Tylosin tartrate 500mg/litre water for 5 days. Alternative: Doxycycline 20mg/kg for 5-7 days. Enrofloxacin effective but reserve for resistant cases. Treat entire flock.
biosecurity_actions: Improve ventilation immediately
Reduce stocking density
Reduce dust and ammonia levels
Source replacement stock from MG-free flocks only
Mycoplasma is egg-transmitted — avoid breeding from affected hens
diseases.prevention: Source MG-free chicks. Maintain good ventilation. Reduce stressors. MG live vaccine available — consult veterinarian.
diseases.vaccination_notes: MG live vaccine (6/85 or ts-11 strain) available. Used mainly in layer breeding flocks. Vaccination does not eliminate the organism — reduces clinical signs only.
diseases.when_to_call_vet: If no improvement after 5 days of antibiotic treatment or if concurrent infection with Newcastle or IB is suspected.
diseases.mortality_rate: Low mortality but severe production and weight gain losses

diseases.name: Aspergillosis
symptoms: white spots on lung at necropsy
distinguishing_symptoms: gasping in young chicks under 10 days
white spots on lung at necropsy
diseases.first_aid: Remove source of mould immediately. Replace all litter. Discard mouldy feed. Improve ventilation in brooder. Antifungal treatment with Amphotericin B or Nystatin under veterinary guidance.
diseases.treatment: Copper sulphate 1:2000 in drinking water for 3 days. Nystatin in feed. Amphotericin B for severe cases under veterinary guidance. Remove mouldy feed and litter immediately.
biosecurity_actions: Remove and replace all mouldy litter immediately
Discard any mouldy or damp feed
Fumigate brooder before placing new chicks
Ensure good ventilation in brooder
Do not use sawdust or wood shavings from unknown sources
diseases.prevention: Use clean dry litter from trusted sources. Store feed dry and use within recommended period. Fumigate brooder before new placement. Ensure adequate ventilation.
diseases.vaccination_notes: No vaccine available. Prevention through biosecurity and litter management is the only effective approach.
diseases.when_to_call_vet: If chick mortality exceeds 10% or if adult birds are affected.
diseases.mortality_rate: Up to 50% in severely affected chick batches
diseases.zoonotic_note: Aspergillus fumigatus can cause pulmonary aspergillosis in immunocompromised humans. Avoid inhaling mouldy litter dust. Wear a face mask when handling mouldy material.

diseases.name: Egg Drop Syndrome
distinguishing_symptoms: sudden drop in egg production with no other illness
diseases.first_aid: No treatment. Confirm diagnosis. Review vaccination history. Supplement diet with calcium and Vitamin D3. Check feed formulation.
diseases.treatment: No specific treatment. Supportive: calcium supplementation, Vitamin D3. Ensure correct feed formulation for laying birds. Egg production typically recovers in 4-8 weeks.
biosecurity_actions: Remove affected eggs from hatchery use immediately
Do not use eggs from affected flock for hatching
Prevent wild duck and waterfowl access to farm — primary reservoir
diseases.prevention: Vaccinate all layer replacements with inactivated EDS-76 vaccine at 14-18 weeks before onset of lay. This is the primary prevention.
diseases.vaccination_notes: Inactivated oil-emulsion EDS-76 vaccine given once at 14-18 weeks via intramuscular injection. Highly effective. Often combined with ND and IB in multivalent vaccines.
diseases.when_to_call_vet: If egg production does not recover within 8 weeks or if differential diagnosis with IB or ND is needed.
